newsitem.title: BELGIUM: U.S. reiterates that EU grain subsidies distort trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. reiterates that EU grain subsidies distort trade.

text.p: Grain export subsidies distort trade and are unnecessary, U.S. officials said after talks with the European Commission.
"We felt subsidies distort markets and there was no real need for the EU to subsidise," said an official. "We expressed concern but there was no threat or anything."
A Commission official said earlier that the EU did not want to flood the world market to dispose of a bumper harvest, nor did it want to restart a grain subsidy war.
The main issue for Washington was to try to speed up EU approval of biotech maize before the crop is harvested.

But U.S. Agriculture Department senior trade adviser Paul Drazek earlier told USDA radio that the EU was still studying whether to approve genetically-altered corn and indicated that a decision would not come in the near term.
U.S. officials added that both sides did, however, agree on the need to conclude a veterinary equivalency agreement by the end of the year and to resolve some extremely complex issues.
The agreement, which involves mutual recognition of animal and plant health standards, covers trade in live animals, fresh and processed meat, pet food and other categories.
"It's a very sensitive issue, especially in view of mad cow disease," noted the official.
A Commission official said it was important that Washington recognise the EU as a bloc and accept to regionalise animal health measures.
A consolidated text may be drawn up by the end of the week.

Talks were held on other farm trade issues, such as wheat gluten, EU rice imports and implementation of a deal under GATT to compensate U.S. exporters for losses after Sweden, Finland and Austria raised import duties after joining the EU in 1995.
"Varying degrees of progress were made," said the official.
